authoredPrompt: This figure is a schematic of a single array drawn as a long horizontal strip of equal cells, shaded to mark off four regions. Four italic labels sit above the strip: p over the leftmost cell, i over the fourth cell, j further to the right, and r over the rightmost cell. Three heavy black bars stand between cells as the region boundaries. The four cells from p through i are pale gray; the six cells between the first and second bar are a darker gray; the five cells after the second bar and before the last are white and empty; and the single cell at the right end, under r, is white and holds the italic letter x. Three curly braces beneath the strip label the pale gray stretch as at most x, written with the symbol for less than or equal to followed by x, the dark gray stretch as greater than x, and the white stretch as unrestricted. The shading separates the portion of the array already classified against the pivot from the portion not yet examined. The strip states the invariant holding at the top of each iteration while a subarray is rearranged in place around the pivot value stored at position r.
authoredInteractions:
- Code editor for PARTITION(A, p, r): learner implements the loop using pivot x, indices i and j, compare(A[j], x), and swap primitives; each executed line advances the strip boundaries and updates the <= x, > x, and unrestricted regions.
- Step-through invariant view: before and after every loop iteration, the diagram highlights which cells satisfy the invariant A[p..i] <= x, A[i+1..j-1] > x, and A[j..r-1] unrestricted.
- Test-case toggle: switch the current A[j] between <= x and > x cases to see why one branch swaps and advances i while the other only advances j.

discrepancies: The default (step-0) strip is rendered at roughly half width on the left with a large code-editor control panel filling the right half, so the overall canvas composition differs from the source's full-width standalone strip (the strip's internal proportions, cell counts, and zone boundaries are nonetheless exact).

The 'j' top label is centered over the first white cell (index 10) while its heavy boundary bar sits at the left edge of that cell; in the source the 'j' glyph hugs the bar more tightly. Minor alignment nit.

Cell values are hidden in the default state (matching the source's empty cells), which is correct, but means the rich numeric playback only becomes visible after pressing Run — a user glancing at the static default sees no demonstration of the invariant in action.
evaluation.notes: The default array strip is a near-exact reproduction of CLRS Fig 7.2 — 16 cells split 4 pale / 6 dark / 5 white + pivot 'x', with correct p/i/j/r italic-serif labels, heavy boundary bars at i, j-1 and r-1, and the three braces '≤ x', '> x', 'unrestricted' spanning the right zones — and it is wrapped in a genuinely deep, concept-correct code workbench (editable partition(), worker-based frame capture, step/play playback, sample/buggy/starter tabs, and a small/large A[j] toggle) that demonstrates the loop invariant and even a missing-inc_i bug; the only real weakness is that the heavy right-hand control panel shrinks and left-aligns the strip so the at-a-glance composition no longer reads as the wide standalone source figure.
action_items: Give the array strip more horizontal room in the default (not-running) state — e.g. let it span the full container width and only dock the code panel to a side column once a run starts — so the static view matches the source's full-width composition.
Align the 'j' (and 'i'/'r') top labels to sit immediately adjacent to their heavy boundary bars as in the source, rather than centered over the next cell.
Optionally pre-populate one worked frame (or a 'show invariant zones' toggle) so the ≤ / > / unrestricted relationship is visible without first pressing Run.

feedback.rationale: With an overall average of 4.8, no failure modes, perfect scores on geometry, interactivity, labels, and concept accuracy, and only minor cosmetic layout nits remaining, the figure is excellent and further iteration is unlikely to yield meaningful improvement.
